title: The Long Bounty
subtitle: From the Brazos to the Rio Grande, April and May 1874

listing.title: The Long Bounty 🌵
listing.blurb: Texas, spring 1874: a $2,000 dead-or-alive poster, a name, and six hundred miles of trail from the Brazos to the Rio Grande. Ford rivers in flood, ride with a cattle drive for cover, and walk into a border town with two sheriffs on one bank and its own government on the other. The man on the poster isn't what it says he is, and the men who wrote it are riding a day behind you. When you finally catch him, you'll have to decide what he's worth. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: Texas in the spring of 1874 is a state changing hands. In January the Reconstruction governor left the capitol and the new Democratic administration moved in; the State Police, the integrated force that answered to him, had already been disbanded the year before; in county after county the men who lost the war are taking back the courthouses, and the men and women who were freed by it are finding out what their deeds, their votes and their testimony are worth. On the Brazos, in Lockett County, the Republican county judge, Nathaniel Brisco, is shot dead in his study on the night of Sunday 5 April, and his young deputy, Clell Ruckert, the new sheriff's nephew, is shot dead in the judge's hall. Within two days a poster is on every courthouse door and stage station between the Red River and the Gulf: $2,000 REWARD, DEAD OR ALIVE, for ISOM HAYWOOD, a colored man, former sergeant of the 9th Cavalry and private of the late State Police, the judge's own bailiff, for the two murders and the robbery of $6,000 of county money. The reward is offered by the Lockett County Stock Association, Colonel Lucius Vandiver, chairman. The party, six people who each have their own reasons to want two thousand dollars, arrive in the county seat of Bascom's Ferry on Wednesday 15 April, ten days behind the man. The trail runs southwest, across the Colorado in spring flood, through the brush country with a Tejana ranchera's cattle drive heading home to the Nueces Strip, across the waterless Wild Horse Desert, to Crow's Ford on the Rio Grande, a border town where two men both claim to be sheriff and the town across the river has its own alcalde, its own army captain and its own opinion of Texans with posters. At the end of it is Palomas Bend, a stone house in a bend of the river, a wife and two children, and Isom Haywood, fevered from a rifle ball nobody has dug out of him, with an oilcloth packet under his hearthstone. The poster is a lie. Isom did not kill the judge. He killed Deputy Ruckert in the judge's hall, in the act of the deputy and a hired gun murdering the judge to take that packet, which holds proof that Colonel Vandiver, the county clerk and a railroad land agent stole the land of the freedmen's settlement at Jubilee with forged tax sales, and that Vandiver's 'rifle club' burned the Jubilee schoolhouse, polling place and church on election night in December, killing an old deacon and a thirteen-year-old boy. Isom is carrying it to the one federal officer the judge trusted, the United States Commissioner at Rio Grande City, before a federal grand jury sits at Brownsville on Monday 1 June. The men who wrote the poster are following the party, a day behind, because they want the packet more than the man, and because a public bounty puts a dozen trackers on the trail for them. Scenarios: the poster and the start in Bascom's Ferry; the trail and the drive; the border town; and the man at the end, and what the party does with him. The campaign does not decide whether the party collects the bounty. It makes sure they know exactly what they would be collecting it for.
hook: Bascom's Ferry, Lockett County, Texas, Wednesday 15 April 1874, an hour before sundown. The Brazos is brown and high and the ferry is running late. On the courthouse door, under a notice of a sheriff's sale and over a lost-mule card, a printed poster in black letters a hand high: $2,000 REWARD. DEAD OR ALIVE. ISOM HAYWOOD. Somebody has already drawn a noose in the margin in pencil, and somebody else has rubbed it half out with a thumb. Two thousand dollars is a farm, a debt paid, a church rebuilt, a stake for the rest of your life. It is also, the man at the livery tells you, about what Colonel Vandiver spends on whiskey in a year, and the colonel is receiving bounty hunters at the Stock Association office tonight, one party at a time, with a description, a letter of authority and fifty dollars against the reward for anyone he thinks can do the job. The man has ten days' start. Six hundred miles of Texas lie between the Brazos and the Rio Grande. Somewhere behind you, though you do not know it yet, a dozen riders are already saddling up to follow whoever looks most likely to find him.

setting.name: Texas, from the Brazos to the Rio Grande, Wednesday 15 April to Monday 18 May 1874
setting.description: Lockett County, Bascom's Ferry, the settlement of Jubilee, Bauer's Ferry, Rancho San Lázaro, Crow's Ford, Villa del Cuervo and Palomas Bend are fictional; the year and the history are real. In January 1874 Governor Edmund J. Davis, a Unionist Republican, gave up the capitol after the disputed December election and Richard Coke's Democrats took the state; the State Police, created under Davis in 1870 and integrated, was abolished in April 1873; the federal Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871 make a conspiracy to deprive citizens of their rights, including by terror at the polls, a federal crime, and federal courts in Texas still sit; and along the lower Rio Grande, in the country between the Nueces and the river that Texans call the Nueces Strip, two years of cattle raiding in both directions across the border, by Anglo cow hunters and by men from across the river alike, have stripped ranches on both banks and made every stranger with a rope suspect. Real public figures (the governor, the president of Mexico, the commanders of real forts) exist only in passing and never appear. Lockett County lies on the Brazos below Waco: cotton bottoms worked by freedmen on shares, cattle on the post-oak uplands, a ferry, a courthouse square and the surveyors' stakes of the Brazos & Gulf Railway, a fictional line that will reach the county next year and make whoever owns the land by its depot rich. South and west of it the trail crosses the Colorado below Austin, the German farms and the Guadalupe hills, the San Antonio road, the brush country of mesquite and prickly pear, the Nueces, and the Wild Horse Desert, a hundred miles of sand and grass where the water holes are a day apart if you know them and further if you don't. Crow's Ford sits on the Texas bank of the Rio Grande forty miles above Rio Grande City and Fort Ringgold; Villa del Cuervo faces it across the river in the state of Tamaulipas; Palomas Bend is twelve miles upriver.
setting.atmosphere: Distance. The campaign should feel long: say the miles aloud, the days, the water left in the canteens, the state of the horses' feet. Spring rain on the Brazos and the Colorado, red mud to the fetlocks, then the brush country drying out under a white sky, then the sand of the desert and a heat that sits on the back of the neck like a hand. Cattle: the lowing of eighteen hundred head bedded down, the smell of dust and dung and crushed mesquite, vaqueros singing to the herd on night watch in Spanish. Campfires, coffee boiled black, bacon, beans, tortillas on a comal, a mouth organ, a guitar, the stars thick enough to read by. Towns are small, wary and loud with news: every stage station has heard of the poster and every saloon has a theory. The tone is a western paperback, not a massacre: gunfights are short and frightening, a man shot is a man hurt, and the dead are buried with names. Let the land be the antagonist: rivers that rise in an hour, a norther that drops the temperature thirty degrees by noon, a horse that goes lame at the worst moment. Let the people be people: Tejano rancheros and vaqueros, German ferrymen, freedmen farmers and preachers, Mexican officials and ferrywomen, Anglo sheriffs good and bad, each with their own stake in what the party does. The poster should follow the party like a smell: every time someone reads it aloud, the players should hear it a little differently.

regions.name: Lockett County and the Brazos
regions.description: Bascom's Ferry, the county seat: a limestone courthouse on a square of chinaberry trees, two saloons (the Brazos House and the Lone Star), a livery, a blacksmith, the Clarion print shop, the Lockett County Bank, a Methodist church for the white town and, a mile out on Mill Creek, the freedmen's settlement of Jubilee: thirty-one homesteads, a church, a burned schoolhouse and a graveyard with two new graves. Colonel Lucius Vandiver's Oakmere plantation lies upriver, cotton and cattle and the big white house. The Brazos & Gulf Railway has its land office in a new frame building by the river, with a survey map in the window.

regions.name: The Colorado and the Hill Country Edge
regions.description: Three to four days' ride southwest. The Colorado below Austin, crossed at Bauer's Ferry, a German family's flatboat ferry on a cable, with a store, a stable and a beer garden under the pecans. German and Czech farms, stone houses, Unionist memories and no love for vigilance committees. In late April the river is in flood.

regions.name: The Brush Country and the Drive
regions.description: South of San Antonio: mesquite, huisache, prickly pear and live oak mottes, the Atascosa, the Frio and the Nueces. Here Doña Refugio Ancira's herd of eighteen hundred head is moving south at ten miles a day to restock Rancho San Lázaro near the Rio Grande, with a remuda of a hundred horses, a chuck wagon and too few hands. Below the Nueces, the Wild Horse Desert: a hundred miles of sand, grass and salt lakes with water holes a hard day apart.

regions.name: The Rio Grande
regions.description: Crow's Ford on the Texas bank: an adobe and stone town of eight hundred, a customs house, a plaza, a church, a jail held by one sheriff and a courthouse held by another, Zenaida Arizpe's ferry and the stage road downriver to Rio Grande City and Fort Ringgold. Villa del Cuervo on the Mexican bank: older, larger, a plaza with a bandstand, the alcalde's casa municipal and a small garrison under a captain who has orders from Ciudad Victoria and opinions of his own. Upriver, the ranchos of the old Spanish grants, and Palomas Bend, where Isom Haywood built a stone house for his wife in 1871.

campaignRules.name: The Riders Behind
campaignRules.description: The pursuers' clock. Colonel Vandiver's son, Garrett Vandiver, leads nine men of the Lockett County Rifles and the hired gun Lyman Gattis a day or so behind the party from the morning they leave Bascom's Ferry. They are not hunting Isom Haywood; they are following the people most likely to find him, so that when he is found they can take the packet he carries and leave no one who has read it. Track the GAP openly, in days, from 0 to 4, on a card the players can see (they may not know at first what it measures; tell them only 'the gap'). It starts at 1 when the party rides out. Each day of travel, adjust it: +1 for hiding the trail well (a Survival check DC 14 by the party's best tracker, made once a day; Ramona Zertuche or Saturnino Ybarra can make it with advantage in country they know); +1 for a hard day's ride the Riders cannot match (frontier.json trail_travel, fast pace, with its exhaustion and horse costs); +2, once, for joining Doña Refugio's drive, since the Riders are looking for half a dozen riders and not for hands among eighteen hundred cattle; +1 for a false trail or a lie that holds (a successful Deception DC 13 at a stage station, ferry or store the Riders will ask at); -1 for a loud day (a gunfight, a brawl, a poker game the whole town talks about, a telegram sent in the party's own names); -1 for a day lost to weather, a flood or a lame horse while the Riders keep moving; -1 each time Josiah Fenner's money buys information ahead of the party. At GAP 0, the Riders are close enough to see the party's dust and will close in at the next stop where the party is distracted. At GAP 4, they have lost the party entirely and go by the main road to Crow's Ford, arriving a full day after the party. The gap matters most at the end: when the party reaches Palomas Bend (lb-scenario-004), the GAP is the number of half-days the party has with Isom before the Riders ride up the bend (0 means they arrive together). Reveal the Riders gradually: dust on the horizon in lb-scenario-001, a stranger asking questions at Bauer's Ferry in lb-scenario-002, nine men at the edge of the herd's firelight, Garrett Vandiver walking into the Crow's Ford cantina in lb-scenario-003.

campaignRules.name: The Long Road
campaignRules.description: The trail is the antagonist. Use frontier.json trail_travel, horses_and_mounts and weather_and_water in full and track them openly: miles covered, days, water (each person and horse needs water every day; a canteen is a day for a person, a horse needs eight gallons and will drink a creek dry), forage, and each horse's condition. Normal pace is 30 to 35 miles a day on good road for riders; the herd makes 10 to 12; the desert halves anything. Each day roll once on a trail events table (frontier.json) or use the scenario's own; each night ask who stands watch. Getting lost is a Survival check (DC 10 on a road, 13 in the brush, 16 in the desert or at night) and costs a day and water, not the campaign. Rivers are obstacles with rules: a ford is a Riding or Animal Handling check, a swim is Athletics, a flood is a set piece (lb-scenario-002). Heat, a norther, a dust storm and thirst give exhaustion as frontier.json weather_and_water describes; Frontier-Born characters are hard to wear down, and they should feel it. A horse that dies under a rider is a hard loss and a long walk: let it happen if the dice say so, and let the next horse be a person's gift. Distances, roughly: Bascom's Ferry to Bauer's Ferry 100 miles; to the Atascosa 110 more; to the Nueces 60; across the Wild Horse Desert to Crow's Ford 110; Palomas Bend 12 miles upriver; Rio Grande City 40 miles down. By the long way the party will actually ride, near six hundred.

campaignRules.name: Dead or Alive
campaignRules.description: The poster has power and so does what people think of the party. Use frontier.json wanted_and_bounties and reputation. ISOM HAYWOOD is at Wanted: dead or alive from the first scene; every bounty hunter, sheriff and stage keeper in Texas has seen his description, and the Thale brothers, three professional manhunters from Fort Worth, are in the race too. Track the party's REPUTATION openly in each place they stay long enough to be known (Bascom's Ferry, Jubilee, Bauer's Ferry, the drive, Crow's Ford, Villa del Cuervo), from -5 to +5. Most places start at 0; Jubilee starts at -1 (bounty hunters), Villa del Cuervo at -1 (armed Texans). The party can be Wanted too: breaking a prisoner out, shooting a deputy or a Rifle, or taking Isom across the river makes the party Wanted: local in that county at once and Wanted: territorial within two weeks if the Vandivers have a reason to print a second poster with their names on it. Payment of the bounty is the poster's own fine print: on delivery of Haywood or proof of his death to Sheriff Dade Ruckert, Lockett County. Nobody pays $2,000 at the Rio Grande except Josiah Fenner, out of a valise, in exchange for the packet, and Fenner does not intend the people he pays to live long.

campaignRules.name: Three Clues
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the party must reach to understand the campaign (Isom did not murder the judge; the poster-writers are hiding a land fraud and a burning; Isom is going home and to the federal commissioner; the Riders are following the party; Gattis is the judge's killer) has at least three clues pointing to it, in different places and scenarios, listed under controlFile.clues and in each scenario's conclusions. Core clues are found automatically by anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill; rolls add detail and speed. A failed roll costs time (and so GAP), water or Reputation, never the case. When the table is stuck, have a companion lay out what the party knows around a campfire.

campaignRules.name: Two Banks
campaignRules.description: Tejano and Mexican characters are full people with their own stakes, on both banks, and the GM should play them that way. Doña Refugio Ancira is restocking a ranch two years of raiding emptied and fighting a lawsuit over her family's grant; Saturnino Ybarra wants the herd home and his son out of a San Antonio jail; Sheriff Matías Uresti of Crow's Ford was appointed under the old government and will not hand his jail to the new one without a court; Zenaida Arizpe runs the ferry and wants both banks to honor her license; the alcalde of Villa del Cuervo, Don Evaristo Lozano, is a lawyer with a list of cattle stolen from his side by Texans and no patience for Texans who want favors; Capitán Severo Galván commands a garrison with orders not to let armed foreigners cross. None of them is a bandit, a comic, or an obstacle for its own sake, and the raiders the party hears about came from both sides of the river. The law is different on each bank: a Texas poster is paper in Villa del Cuervo, and taking a man across the river by force is kidnapping on both sides. Mexico will not hand Isom to Texas on a poster, and everyone on the Mexican bank knows it.

wildernessStarts.label: Bascom's Ferry: the courthouse door, Wednesday at sundown
Crow's Ford: the plaza at noon, two sheriffs and a ferry
Palomas Bend: a stone house, a rifle on the roof

explorationRules: This is a road campaign and the map runs from the Brazos in the northeast to the Rio Grande in the southwest. Between the scenarios' set pieces the unit of time is the travel day: say the date, the miles, the weather, the water and the gap (campaignRules, The Riders Behind) at the start of every day, roll or choose one trail event, and ask who stands the night watch. Use frontier.json trail_travel, horses_and_mounts and weather_and_water for every leg, and let the players make real choices about route: the main road through San Antonio is faster and full of people who have seen the poster; the brush trails are slower, drier and quieter; the drive is slowest of all and hides them best. In towns the unit of time is the scene, about two hours, and towns are small sandboxes of named people listed in each scenario, each acting on what they could know. Investigation follows the three-clue rule (campaignRules): core clues are automatic for anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill; failed rolls cost time, water, Reputation or the gap, never the case. Fights are short and should feel dangerous; most have a way to be talked out of, ridden away from or never started, and frontier.json showdowns gives the stare-down before the draw. Money is real and scarce: a meal is two bits, a night at a hotel a dollar, a box of cartridges a dollar and a half, a good horse a hundred; drovers earn thirty dollars a month. Let the party feel the weight of two thousand dollars every time they count what they have left. Between scenes let the country breathe: a scissor-tail flycatcher on a fence post, a norther coming as a blue line on the horizon, a German farmer's wife selling eggs at a ford, a vaquero's song, an old freedman fishing the Brazos who saw which way the judge's bailiff rode and is not telling bounty hunters, a Mexican family crossing at a ford to visit cousins as if the river were a street.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, this does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Lockett County, Bascom's Ferry, Jubilee, the Brazos & Gulf Railway, Bauer's Ferry, Rancho San Lázaro, Crow's Ford, Villa del Cuervo, Palomas Bend and every named person are fictional. The end of Reconstruction in Texas, the abolition of the State Police, the Enforcement Acts, the federal court at Brownsville, Fort Ringgold, the 9th Cavalry's service in Texas, election violence in 1873, fraudulent tax sales against freedmen's land, and two-way cattle raiding on the lower Rio Grande in the early 1870s are real history. No real person appears as a character.
controlFile.theTruth: In the summer of 1873 the Brazos & Gulf Railway surveyed its line through Lockett County and chose a depot site on Mill Creek, in the middle of Jubilee, a settlement of thirty-one freedmen's homesteads bought with wages and Freedmen's Bureau help between 1867 and 1870. Josiah Fenner, the railway's land agent, told Colonel Lucius Vandiver, chairman of the Lockett County Stock Association and of the county Democratic committee, where the depot would go, in exchange for a share. Vandiver had the county clerk, Orrin Spratt, alter the 1872 and 1873 tax rolls to show the Jubilee lands delinquent, though every family had paid and held receipts signed by the old tax collector, and on Monday 3 November 1873 the sheriff of the day, who was leaving office and did as he was told, sold all thirty-one homesteads at a tax sale on the courthouse steps to L. Vandiver for $1,240. Jubilee's people were not told; the notices were posted where they could not see them. On election day, Tuesday 2 December 1873, Jubilee's schoolhouse, which was also its church and the county's Precinct 4 polling place, was set on fire after dark with the ballot box inside, by riders of Vandiver's 'Lockett County Rifles', a rifle club of his foremen, tenants' sons and friends; the precinct judge, Deacon Caesar Lytle, aged 61, went in for the box and died, and his grandson Henry, 13, went in after him and died too. Isom Haywood, a deputy sheriff and the county judge's bailiff, who had been sent to keep the peace at the polls, saw the riders by the light of the fire and knew two of them: Vandiver's son Garrett, who sat his horse at the edge of the firelight and did not ride in, and a hired man named Lyman Gattis, who threw the lamp. The burning made Precinct 4's votes disappear; the county went Democratic by forty votes; Dade Ruckert, the Rifles' captain before Garrett, was elected sheriff and took office in February 1874. In February the Jubilee families found they no longer owned their land and County Judge Nathaniel Brisco, a Unionist appointed under the old government whose term had months left, started to build a case. He got Spratt's original tax roll entries and the Jubilee receipts, the tax-sale deeds, a letter from Fenner to Vandiver about 'the Mill Creek price' that a railway clerk sold him for $50, and sworn statements from nine Jubilee witnesses and from Isom about election night, and on Monday 2 March learned that Vandiver had sold the Jubilee lands to the Brazos & Gulf Land Company for $41,000. Because the new state government would not touch it, and because the federal Enforcement Acts make it a federal crime, he wrote on 21 March to his oldest friend and former law partner, Abner Ruthven, United States Commissioner at Rio Grande City, that he would send 'the whole of it, by a man I trust with my life' in time for the federal grand jury at Brownsville on Monday 1 June. Spratt read the press copy of that letter in the judge's letterbook in the clerk's office, and told Vandiver. On the night of Sunday 5 April, Vandiver sent Gattis and Deputy Clell Ruckert, the sheriff's nephew and the colonel's own sister's son, to take the packet and kill the judge. Gattis shot Brisco through his study window with a repeating rifle; Clell Ruckert came in through the kitchen to take the packet from the desk; Isom, arriving with his saddlebags packed to leave at dawn, came in at the front door, met Clell in the hall with the packet in one hand and a revolver in the other, and they fired together. Clell died; Isom took a ball from Gattis's rifle through the window in his left side as he knelt by the judge. Brisco lived long enough to say, in front of his housekeeper, Mrs. Lovisa Dunagan, 'Go, Isom. Take it to Abner. Don't let them have it.' Isom went. In the morning, Sheriff Ruckert's justice of the peace held an inquest in an hour, and the county treasurer's safe was found open with $6,000 missing; Spratt and Vandiver had taken that money over the winter and the 'robbery' covered it. Vandiver had the poster printed on Tuesday 7 April, offering $1,000 from the Stock Association, $500 from the county and $500 'from friends of law and order', which is the Brazos & Gulf Railway, through Fenner. A public bounty does what Vandiver wants: it puts every manhunter in Texas on Isom's trail, it makes his story worthless, and it means that when somebody finds him, the Rifles can be there. Garrett Vandiver, who believes Isom murdered his cousin Clell (which is true) and the judge (which is not), and who has told himself for five months that the fire was an accident, leads nine Rifles and Gattis after whichever bounty hunters look most likely to succeed. That is the party. Isom, wounded, rode southwest by night, crossed the Colorado at Bauer's Ferry on Thursday 9 April as it began to rise, pulled the ferryman's grandson out of the water, reached the herd his wife's aunt, Doña Refugio Ancira, was gathering on the Cibolo on Monday 13 April, took a fresh horse and her blessing, and reached his own homestead at Palomas Bend on the Rio Grande on Saturday 25 April, where his wife Inés and their two children had gone in December. The ball is still in him; the wound has gone bad; he has been in bed with fever for two weeks. Ruthven is in Brownsville preparing for the grand jury and returns to Rio Grande City on Monday 18 May. Isom means to ride to him that day, if he can sit a horse. Inés wants him to cross the river to her cousins in Villa del Cuervo with the children and never come back.
controlFile.theMan: Isom Haywood, 38, born enslaved on Lucius Vandiver's Oakmere plantation on the Brazos in 1836, freed in June 1865, enlisted in the 9th Cavalry in 1866, served as a sergeant at Fort Brown and Fort Ringgold on the Rio Grande from 1867 to 1871, where he met and married Inés Cantú, a schoolteacher from Palomas Bend, and bought 160 acres of her family's old grant land with his savings. Mustered out in 1871, he joined the State Police and was posted to Lockett County because no one else would take it; when the State Police was abolished he became a deputy sheriff and Judge Brisco's bailiff. Six foot one, a scar through the left eyebrow from a horse thief's quirt, a deep slow voice, a habit of saying exactly what he means. He is not a saint: he killed Clell Ruckert, he knew he might have to, and he would do it again; he left a dying man because the man told him to; he has brought his trouble home to his wife and children, and he knows it. He is not what the poster says. He is a witness, the last lawman Jubilee had, and a frightened, stubborn, feverish man who wants to see his children grow up and is not sure he can do that and keep his word to the judge at the same time.
thePosterWriters: Colonel Lucius Vandiver, 63, Oakmere: planter, cattleman, chairman of the Lockett County Stock Association and of the county Democratic committee; the money and the will behind the fraud, the fire and the murder. Courteous, generous, certain that what he did was the restoration of order. He does not leave Lockett County; he sends his son, his money and Gattis.

Orrin Spratt, 47, county clerk: altered the tax rolls, read the judge's letterbook and told Vandiver, and helped empty the treasury over the winter. A frightened bookkeeper in sleeve garters; the weakest link, and he knows it.

Josiah Fenner, 41, land agent of the Brazos & Gulf Railway: sold Vandiver the depot site, bought the Jubilee land back for the company at $41,000 and kept a commission from both ends. Follows the party south by stage and telegraph with $5,000 of railway money in a valise, to buy the packet or the people who have it. A cheerful, plump, reasonable man in a linen duster who never touches a gun and is the most dangerous negotiator in the campaign.

Sheriff Dade Ruckert, 50, Lockett County: former captain of the Rifles, elected in December on the burned precinct, Clell's uncle. Stays in Bascom's Ferry. His grief for his nephew is real; so is his part in the rest.

Garrett Vandiver, 29, the colonel's son, captain of the Lockett County Rifles: leads the Riders. Rode with his father's cavalry escort as a boy at the end of the war and has never been allowed to be anything but his father's son. He sat his horse at the edge of the firelight at Jubilee and has told himself the fire was meant to scare. He believes Isom murdered both men. He is the campaign's turnable heart: shown the truth, he may break, or he may not.

Lyman Gattis, about 40, the hired gun: killed the judge, threw the lamp at Jubilee, and rides with Garrett's Riders as their 'tracker'. Pale-eyed, quiet, polite to women and horses, rides a grey with a bar shoe on the near fore. He has a Missouri past and a Red River past and has killed men in both. He will kill Isom, anyone who has read the packet, and, if it comes to it, Garrett.
redHerrings: The missing $6,000. Everyone assumes Isom took it; the poster says so. He never saw it. Spratt's and Vandiver's winter withdrawals took it; the safe was opened with the treasurer's key, not forced.

The Thale brothers, three professional bounty hunters from Fort Worth, are ahead of the party on the road, behind it, and at the river crossing, and look like the pursuers. They are rivals, not the Riders: hard men in a hard trade who want the money and nothing else, and who can be outbid, outridden, outtalked, or, if the party proves the poster is a lie, turned into reluctant witnesses.

Doña Refugio Ancira lies to the party about Isom from the moment she hears the name. She is not an accomplice to murder; she is a woman protecting her niece's husband, and once she trusts the party she is their strongest ally on the border.

Sheriff Hollan Purcell of Crow's Ford, the new government's man, looks like Vandiver's agent. He is not; he has never met Vandiver. He is an ambitious, frightened man who has been told by letter that a murderer's in-laws live in his county, and who wants the arrest that will make his claim to the office stick.

Inés Haywood's brother, Dámaso Cantú, held by Purcell in Crow's Ford as an 'accessory', looks like the key to finding Isom. He is a bait the Riders mean to use; he will tell the party nothing until they have proved they are not hunting his sister's husband.
clues: A. ISOM DID NOT MURDER JUDGE BRISCO. A1: the undertaker, Hiram Tisdale, kept the ball he dug out of the judge: a .44 rimfire rifle bullet; Isom carried an Army revolver (.45) and a Spencer carbine (.56) and the poster says so (lb-scenario-001). A2: the judge's study window: the glass broke inward onto his desk; he was shot from outside, while Mrs. Dunagan heard Isom at the front door (lb-scenario-001). A3: Mrs. Lovisa Dunagan, the housekeeper, heard the judge's last words: 'Go, Isom. Take it to Abner. Don't let them have it' (lb-scenario-001). A4: under the study window, in the flowerbed, the prints of a horse with a bar shoe on the near fore; the blacksmith, Gus Ekholm, put that shoe on a grey for 'Colonel Vandiver's new man' in March (lb-scenario-001). A5: Gottfried Bauer at the Colorado: Isom was shot in the side and bleeding when he crossed, and still went into the river after a drowning boy (lb-scenario-002). A6: Isom's own account and the packet (lb-scenario-004).

B. THE POSTER-WRITERS ARE HIDING A LAND FRAUD. B1: the Jubilee families' 1872 and 1873 tax receipts, kept by Mother Hagar Lytle in her Bible (lb-scenario-001). B2: the county tax roll: the Jubilee entries marked delinquent in fresh ink over scraped-out 'pd.' marks (Investigation, automatic if compared with the receipts) (lb-scenario-001). B3: the deed book: thirty-one tax-sale deeds to L. Vandiver on 3 November 1873 for $1,240, and the same land to the Brazos & Gulf Land Company on 2 March 1874 for $41,000 (lb-scenario-001). B4: the railway's survey map in the land office window: the depot is on Mill Creek, in the middle of Jubilee (lb-scenario-001). B5: Vandiver's private offer of another $1,000 'for any papers he carries, unread' and Fenner's later $5,000 (lb-scenario-001, 003). B6: the packet itself (lb-scenario-004).

C. THE RIFLES BURNED THE JUBILEE SCHOOLHOUSE ON ELECTION NIGHT. C1: Reverend Solomon Burris (if played) or Mother Hagar Lytle: riders with flour sacks over their hats, a man who threw a lamp, a horse at the edge of the light that didn't come in (lb-scenario-001). C2: the precinct 4 returns were never counted, and the county went Democratic by forty votes (the Clarion's back numbers) (lb-scenario-001). C3: Wiley Dunmore recognizes Gattis and knows his trick of throwing a lamp to start a fire (lb-scenario-002 or 003). C4: Garrett Vandiver's own guilt: he will not say 'Jubilee' and changes the subject when anyone does (lb-scenario-003). C5: Isom's sworn statement in the packet names Gattis and Garrett (lb-scenario-004).

D. ISOM IS GOING HOME, AND TO THE FEDERAL COMMISSIONER. D1: the press copy of the judge's letter of 21 March to Abner Ruthven, U.S. Commissioner, Rio Grande City, in the judge's letterbook (lb-scenario-001). D2: Quincy Treadwell, the judge's clerk, knows Ruthven and that the packet was meant for him (lb-scenario-001). D3: Isom's landlady at Jubilee or Reverend Burris: his wife and children went home to her people 'on the Rio Grande, up from Rio Grande City' in December (lb-scenario-001). D4: Bauer's Ferry: he asked the road to San Antonio and the Rio Grande (lb-scenario-002). D5: Doña Refugio's vaqueros: the tall Black rider who came to the herd on the Cibolo was 'family' (lb-scenario-002). D6: Crow's Ford: Inés Haywood comes to town for her brother; Zenaida Arizpe knows the way to Palomas Bend (lb-scenario-003).

E. THE RIDERS ARE FOLLOWING THE PARTY, NOT ISOM. E1: dust behind the party on the first day out, and the same nine riders asking about 'a party of hunters' at each stop a day after they pass (lb-scenario-001, 002). E2: a Rifle at Bauer's Ferry asks Gottfried Bauer which way the party went, not which way Isom went (lb-scenario-002). E3: Fenner's telegram, from San Antonio to Garrett at Oakville: 'KEEP BEHIND THEM. THEY WILL FIND HIM. NO ONE TO READ IT' (lb-scenario-002, a talkative telegraph clerk or Fenner's own luggage). E4: Garrett's Riders arrive at Crow's Ford hours after the party (lb-scenario-003).

F. LYMAN GATTIS KILLED THE JUDGE. F1: the bar-shoe grey (A4) among the Riders' horses (lb-scenario-002 or 003). F2: Gattis's repeating rifle is a .44 rimfire; so was the ball in the judge (A1) (lb-scenario-003). F3: Wiley Dunmore knows him from the Red River and has seen him kill (lb-scenario-002 or 003). F4: Isom saw Gattis's face at the window in the lamplight (lb-scenario-004).
controlFile.theFinalChoice: The campaign ends at Palomas Bend with Isom Haywood in the party's hands, alive or dead, and the packet within reach. Every choice is open and every choice has a price. HAND HIM OVER: the bounty is paid only in Bascom's Ferry, to Sheriff Ruckert, and the Riders mean to kill everyone who has read the packet; Fenner will pay $2,000 in cash at the Rio Grande for Isom and $5,000 for the packet, and Gattis will try to take it back on the road. TAKE HIM AND THE PACKET TO RUTHVEN: fifty-two miles down the river road to Rio Grande City with the Riders behind them; Ruthven can take Isom's sworn complaint and put him and the packet under the protection of Fort Ringgold until the grand jury on 1 June. This is the road to justice for Jubilee, and it may hang Isom: he killed a white deputy in Texas, and no federal commissioner can make a Texas indictment disappear. LET HIM CROSS: Villa del Cuervo will shelter Isom and his family and will not hand him to Texas on a poster; the packet can go to Ruthven without him, but without Isom's own testimony the burning and the murder are hearsay, and the fraud alone is a civil suit that will take years. The party's own answer is the end of the campaign: there is no right one, only what they can live with. Isom himself will argue for crossing, Inés harder; the Jubilee families need him to testify; Reverend Burris, if played, has the strongest claim of anyone on what he does.
controlFile.outcomes: ISOM: hanged or shot (if handed over; the Riders do not take him back alive); in Mexico with his family (if he crosses), where he lives to be an old man and never sees the Brazos again; or alive in Rio Grande City under federal protection, testifying in June, and then, likeliest, crossing the river with Ruthven's quiet blessing before Lockett County's indictment for Clell Ruckert can reach him; if the party has also proved the poster a lie, Ruthven can make the case that Clell Ruckert died committing a federal crime, and the state indictment is quietly dropped in 1876. THE PACKET: in Ruthven's hands by 1 June means federal indictments for Lucius Vandiver, Orrin Spratt and Lyman Gattis under the Enforcement Acts, and Fenner testifying against all three to save himself; the Brazos & Gulf Railway, wanting clean title, settles with the Jubilee families for the land's value or gives it back, and the depot is moved a mile east. In Fenner's hands, it is burned in a stage-station stove and Jubilee is gone. GARRETT VANDIVER: dead at Palomas Bend, a witness against his father (if shown the truth and given the chance), or home on the Brazos with a story he will never quite believe. GATTIS: the deadliest single man in the campaign; shot, taken, or gone across the Wild Horse Desert to do it again somewhere else. THE MONEY: if the party takes the right road, there is no $2,000; there may be Doña Refugio's drover's wages ($30 a month each and a horse apiece), a federal posse's per diem from Ruthven ($2 a day), the Thale brothers' respect, Fenner's valise if the party is not honest about it, and the Jubilee congregation's gratitude, which comes in the form of a meal, a song and a name for the new schoolhouse. JUBILEE: the schoolhouse is rebuilt in the summer of 1875, of stone this time; the two graves get headstones; the precinct votes again in November 1874 under federal observers. The question the campaign asks is the one every character has been asking since the courthouse door: what is a man worth, and who gets to say.
